French jewelers rediscovered it in the 1860s.

post.caption: This jewelry enamel has no metal backing. It is called plique-à-jour, which means open to light. Thin wires form tiny cells on a temporary backing, and clear enamel is fused into the cells. Then the backing is removed, sometimes by dissolving it in acid. The result looks like a tiny stained glass window, and light can shine straight through the finished enamel. French jewelers rediscovered it in the 1860s. René Lalique used it in jewelry around the year 1900, and Norwegian firms showed it at the 1900 Paris exhibition. A single piece can take up to four months.
